title: Least-Privilege Tool Scoping and MCP Allow-Listing for a Release-Notes Agent
description: Tests the ability to scope MCP toolsets, network access, and error-handling behavior to what a task actually requires, and to correctly distinguish a transient failure (retry) from a non-transient one (stop and escalate).

scenario.background: Dev, a platform engineer, is configuring a release-notes coding agent. Its job: read merged PRs since the last release, summarize them, and open a draft PR updating CHANGELOG.md. Nothing about the task requires modifying issues, running deployments, or reaching the public internet.

characters.name: Dev Chatterjee
characters.concern: Wants the agent to have exactly the access it needs and nothing more, and to fail loudly and specifically rather than silently or destructively.

characters.name: Priyanka Rao
characters.concern: Suggested a third-party MCP server for changelog formatting found in a public registry.

questions.stem: Which GitHub MCP configuration correctly matches the task's actual needs?
options: Enable the full default GitHub MCP toolset (actions, code_security, pull_requests, issues) so the agent has everything it might need
Enable only the pull_requests toolset, in read-only mode, since the agent only needs to read PR history and diffs and never needs to modify a PR, run deployments, or touch issues
Enable the issues toolset only, since CHANGELOG.md updates are issue-adjacent
Enable the actions toolset, since the agent is part of a CI-like workflow
questions.explanation: B is correct because the task only requires reading PR history and diffs — it never modifies a PR, runs a deployment, or touches issues — so enabling only pull_requests in read-only mode gives the agent exactly what it needs and nothing it doesn't, which is least privilege applied to MCP tool scoping. A grants unrelated, higher-risk toolsets (actions, code_security, issues) the task never uses. C and D each grant a toolset unrelated to the actual task (reading and summarizing PRs).

questions.stem: Priyanka suggests a third-party changelog-formatting MCP server found in a public registry. What should Dev do?
options: Connect it immediately, since it's already listed in a public MCP registry, which implies it's been vetted
File a request for platform-security review before connecting it, since registry presence isn't the same as clearance on the org's approved MCP allow list
Connect it only if Priyanka personally vouches for it
Refuse to consider any third-party MCP server ever, regardless of review process
questions.explanation: B is correct because MCP servers require allow-listing before connection, not disconnection after a problem — registry presence is not equivalent to organizational clearance, so the correct move is routing it through the actual review process before any connection is made. A conflates public discoverability with vetted trust, which are not the same thing. C substitutes informal personal vouching for a real security review process. D is an unnecessary blanket refusal when a legitimate review path exists and should be used.

questions.stem: The org's default network firewall already covers GitHub and the npm registry the formatting script depends on. Should Dev add a broader allowlist entry just in case future needs arise?
options: Yes, broaden the allowlist proactively to avoid needing to make changes later
No — the default firewall already covers what this task actually needs; extending it 'just in case' isn't justified by anything the task requires
Yes, but only if a teammate requests it informally
No, and the existing allowlist should also be reduced further, cutting off the npm registry the task actually needs
questions.explanation: B is correct because network access, like tool access, should be scoped to what a task actually requires — the default firewall already covers GitHub and npm, which is everything this task needs, so adding broader access without a concrete justification violates least privilege for no benefit. A and C both expand access speculatively rather than on demonstrated need. D incorrectly proposes removing access the task genuinely requires (npm, for the formatting script's dependencies).

questions.stem: During a session, the formatting script fails once with an npm registry timeout, then later fails again because a merged PR's title contains characters the formatter can't parse. How should the agent handle each failure?
options: Retry both failures indefinitely until they succeed

Retry the timeout with backoff (transient), but stop and escalate on the parsing failure (non-transient) — leaving a comment on the tracking issue explaining exactly what broke, ending the session in a failed state that triggers a lifecycle alert
Stop and escalate on both failures without attempting any retry
Silently skip both failed steps and continue as if nothing happened
questions.explanation: B is correct because error handling should default to 'stop and escalate' for anything non-transient rather than 'keep trying and hope' — the registry timeout is transient and worth a backoff retry, while the parsing failure is a genuine bug that won't resolve by retrying, so the agent correctly stops, documents exactly what broke, and triggers a lifecycle alert for a human to act on. A wastes time and resources retrying a failure that will never self-resolve. C fails to use a reasonable retry for a genuinely transient issue. D hides a real failure instead of surfacing it, which could let a broken changelog entry slip through unnoticed.

keyLearnings: MCP toolsets should be enabled only for what a task actually requires — starting from an empty allowlist and adding only what's justified by the task, not a broad default trimmed down later.
Registry presence for a third-party MCP server is not the same as organizational clearance — new servers require allow-listing review before connection, never connect-first-review-later.
Network and tool access should not be broadened speculatively 'just in case' — least privilege applies to firewall rules the same way it applies to tool grants.

Error handling should distinguish transient failures (retry with backoff) from non-transient ones (stop, document precisely, and escalate) rather than retrying everything or escalating everything uniformly.
